# Introduction

Vectors hold one type in one dimension. Real data needs bigger containers:

| Container | Holds | Example |
|:----------|:------|:--------|
| **matrix** | one type, rows × columns | a plate of absorbance readings |
| **data frame** | one type *per column* | a patient table |
| **list** | anything | everything about one gene |

In this lab you will:

- create matrices, data frames and lists,
- select values by position, name and condition,
- calculate on rows and columns,
- filter, extend and merge data frames,
- deal with missing values,
- get results out of lists.

<div class="boxy boxy-lightbulb">
As always: predict first, then run. If the output surprises you, find out why. Click the key to reveal example code. Keep your code and notes in your **R Markdown learning journal**.
</div>

# Matrices

A 96-well plate is a matrix: rows A–H, columns 1–12. Here is a small part of one, with absorbance readings for 3 rows and 4 columns, read **row by row**:

```{r}
readings <- c(0.12, 0.45, 0.88, 0.05,
              0.15, 0.51, 0.93, 0.06,
              0.11, 0.48, 0.85, 0.05)
```

1. Create a matrix `plate` from `readings` with 3 rows, filled row by row. Name the rows `"A"`, `"B"`, `"C"` and the columns `"1"` to `"4"`. What are its dimensions? What does `length()` return?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
plate <- matrix(readings, nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(plate) <- c("A", "B", "C")
colnames(plate) <- 1:4
plate
dim(plate)
length(plate)   # total number of values
```

What happens if you leave out `byrow = TRUE`?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
matrix(readings, nrow = 3)   # filled column by column: the values end up in the wrong wells
```

2. Select:
   - the reading in well B3,
   - all of row C,
   - all of column 2,
   - all readings above 0.5.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
plate["B", "3"]
plate["C", ]
plate[, "2"]
plate[plate > 0.5]
```

3. Column 4 is the blank. Subtract the mean of the blank wells from every reading. Then calculate the mean of each column and the maximum of each row.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
blank <- mean(plate[, "4"])
plate_corrected <- plate - blank
round(plate_corrected, 3)
colMeans(plate_corrected)
apply(plate_corrected, 1, max)
```

4. Add a row `"D"` with the readings `0.13, 0.47, 0.90, 0.05`. Then transpose the plate. What happened to the row and column names?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
plate <- rbind(plate, D = c(0.13, 0.47, 0.90, 0.05))
plate
t(plate)   # rows and columns, including their names, swap places
```

5. Try to put the text `"empty"` in well A4. What happens to the whole matrix?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
plate_test <- plate
plate_test["A", "4"] <- "empty"
plate_test       # every value becomes text: a matrix holds one type
```

# Data frames

A small clinical study:

```{r}
patients <- data.frame(
  id     = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05", "P06"),
  age    = c(34, 58, 47, 62, 29, 51),
  sex    = c("F", "M", "M", "F", "F", "M"),
  bmi    = c(22.4, 31.2, 27.8, 29.5, 21.0, 33.1),
  smoker = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  group  = c("drug", "placebo", "drug", "placebo", "placebo", "drug")
)
```

6. How many rows and columns does `patients` have? What type is each column? Get a summary of every column.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
dim(patients)
str(patients)
summary(patients)
```

7. Get:
   - the `bmi` column, with `$` and with `[ , ]`,
   - the rows of patients 2 to 4,
   - the age of the third patient,
   - the mean age.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
patients$bmi
patients[, "bmi"]
patients[2:4, ]
patients[3, "age"]
mean(patients$age)
```

8. Filter the table:
   - all smokers,
   - patients in the drug group who are older than 45,
   - the IDs of patients with a BMI of 30 or more.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
patients[patients$smoker, ]
patients[patients$group == "drug" & patients$age > 45, ]
patients$id[patients$bmi >= 30]
```

9. What is the mean BMI in the drug group? And in the placebo group?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
mean(patients$bmi[patients$group == "drug"])
mean(patients$bmi[patients$group == "placebo"])
```

10. Add two columns:
    - `obese`: `TRUE` if the BMI is 30 or more,
    - `age_months`: the age in months.

    Then make `group` a factor with `"placebo"` as the first level.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
patients$obese <- patients$bmi >= 30
patients$age_months <- patients$age * 12
patients$group <- factor(patients$group, levels = c("placebo", "drug"))
levels(patients$group)
patients
```

11. Blood glucose was measured in a separate lab. Their table is **in a different order**, is missing one patient, and has one patient who is not in your study:

```{r}
glucose <- data.frame(id = c("P04", "P01", "P06", "P02", "P03", "P07"),
                      glucose = c(6.1, 5.2, 7.4, 5.9, NA, 5.5))
```

Merge it with `patients`. Which patients are in the result? Then look up the `all.x` argument in `?merge` to keep all your patients.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
merge(patients, glucose, by = "id")                # only patients in both tables
combined <- merge(patients, glucose, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
combined                                           # P05 is kept, with glucose NA
```

12. In `combined`, how many values are missing in each column? How many complete rows are left after `na.omit()`? What is the mean glucose of the patients who have a value?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
colSums(is.na(combined))
nrow(na.omit(combined))
mean(combined$glucose, na.rm = TRUE)
```

13. R comes with a real life-science data set, `ToothGrowth`: tooth length in 60 guinea pigs given vitamin C as orange juice (`OJ`) or ascorbic acid (`VC`), at three doses. Explore it:
    - How many rows and columns? What are the column types?
    - What is the mean tooth length for each supplement?
    - Show only the rows with the highest dose (2 mg/day).

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
dim(ToothGrowth)
str(ToothGrowth)
mean(ToothGrowth$len[ToothGrowth$supp == "OJ"])
mean(ToothGrowth$len[ToothGrowth$supp == "VC"])
ToothGrowth[ToothGrowth$dose == 2, ]
```

# Lists

14. Create a list `gene` with everything you know about one gene:
    - `symbol`: `"TP53"`,
    - `chromosome`: `17`,
    - `exon_lengths`: `c(103, 22, 279, 184, 113, 110, 137)`,
    - `functions`: `c("DNA repair", "apoptosis", "cell cycle arrest")`,
    - `expression`: a data frame with the columns `tissue` (`"liver"`, `"lung"`, `"skin"`) and `tpm` (`45.2`, `61.8`, `30.1`).

    Look at it with `str()`.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
gene <- list(
  symbol       = "TP53",
  chromosome   = 17,
  exon_lengths = c(103, 22, 279, 184, 113, 110, 137),
  functions    = c("DNA repair", "apoptosis", "cell cycle arrest"),
  expression   = data.frame(tissue = c("liver", "lung", "skin"),
                            tpm    = c(45.2, 61.8, 30.1))
)
str(gene)
```

15. Compare `gene["symbol"]` and `gene[["symbol"]]`. What is the class of each?

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
gene["symbol"]
class(gene["symbol"])     # a list
gene[["symbol"]]
class(gene[["symbol"]])   # the value itself
```

16. Get:
    - the length of the third exon,
    - the total length of all exons,
    - the number of known functions,
    - the TPM in lung.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
gene$exon_lengths[3]
sum(gene$exon_lengths)
length(gene$functions)
gene$expression$tpm[gene$expression$tissue == "lung"]
```

17. Add an element `aliases` with the value `c("p53", "LFS1")`. Then remove `chromosome`. Check the names of the list.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
gene$aliases <- c("p53", "LFS1")
gene$chromosome <- NULL
names(gene)
```

18. Use `t.test()` to compare tooth length between the two supplements in `ToothGrowth`. The result is a list. What are its elements? Get the p-value and the 95% confidence interval.

```{r,accordion=TRUE}
res <- t.test(len ~ supp, data = ToothGrowth)
is.list(res)
names(res)
res$p.value
res$conf.int
```
